title: Theory of Consumer Behaviour
outcomes: Explain the nature and classification of human wants and the meaning of utility.
Relate total and marginal utility and apply the law of diminishing marginal utility with its limitations.
Measure consumer surplus from a schedule and from a demand curve, and state its uses and limitations.
Explain indifference curves, MRS, their properties, the budget line and consumer equilibrium.

meta.exam_tip: Expect MCQs on TU–MU relationships, consumer surplus calculations, IC properties and the equilibrium condition MRSxy = Px/Py. Read whether the question gives MU or TU.

concepts.title: Nature of human wants
body: A want is a desire to own or use goods and services that give satisfaction. Wants arise from physical needs, psychological drives and social pressures. Because resources are limited, we choose between urgent and less urgent wants.

Characteristics: wants are unlimited in number, though each single want can be satisfied (satiable); they differ in intensity; they compete with one another for limited means; some are complementary (a car also needs fuel); a want can be met in alternative ways; wants are subjective and relative, varying with time, place and person; some recur, others do not; wants can turn into habits and customs; and they are shaped by income, taste, fashion, advertising and social norms.

Utility is the want-satisfying power of a commodity. It is a psychological, subjective idea: it is not the same as usefulness and carries no moral judgement — a cigarette has utility to a smoker. Total utility (TU) is the sum of the marginal utilities of all units consumed (TU = ΣMU). Marginal utility (MU) is the extra utility from one more unit: MU = TUn − TUn−1 = ΔTU/ΔN.
concepts.analogy: Wants are like a queue at a ticket counter that never ends; utility is how happy each person is when served.
concepts.work: Consumer research for product launches, which CAs in strategy and FP&A roles rely on, starts from what want the product satisfies and how intense it is.

concepts.title: Classification of wants: necessaries, comforts, luxuries
body: Necessaries are essential for living, in three kinds: necessaries for life (existence) — the minimum food, clothing and shelter needed to stay alive; necessaries for efficiency — nourishing food, adequate clothing, clean water, a decent home, education and recreation that keep a person energetic and productive; conventional necessaries — things we feel compelled to have because of habit or social custom (gifts at festivals, a particular dress at weddings), though they are needed neither for existence nor for efficiency.

Comforts make life comfortable and satisfying — tasty food, a good house, clothes for different occasions, labour-saving appliances. They are less urgent than necessaries. Luxuries are superfluous and expensive — designer clothing, vintage cars, lavish furniture, items of vanity.
The classification is not rigid: what is a luxury for one person or era may be a comfort or necessity for another. Mobile phones and refrigerators moved from luxury to necessity within a generation.
concepts.analogy: Necessaries are the foundation of a house, comforts are the furniture, luxuries are the chandelier.
concepts.work: GST rate slabs broadly follow this logic — essentials at nil or low rates, luxury and "sin" goods at the highest rate plus cess — which CAs apply when classifying goods for clients.

concepts.title: Relationship between TU and MU
body: TU = ΣMU and MU = TUn − TUn−1. At the first unit, TU = MU.
While TU rises at a diminishing rate, MU falls but stays positive. When TU is at its maximum (and constant), MU = 0 — the point of satiety. When TU starts to fall, MU becomes negative (disutility).
On a graph, the TU curve rises, flattens at its peak and then falls; the MU curve slopes downward, cuts the X-axis exactly where TU is maximum and goes below it afterwards.
concepts.analogy: TU is the height of a hill you are climbing; MU is how steep the next step is. At the summit the next step is flat (MU = 0); beyond it you go downhill (negative MU).
concepts.work: The same marginal-vs-total logic is used throughout CA work: marginal cost and total cost, marginal revenue and total revenue, incremental return on extra investment.

concepts.title: Law of diminishing marginal utility
body: Other things remaining the same, as a consumer takes more and more units of a commodity, the extra satisfaction from each successive unit eventually falls. This is the law of diminishing marginal utility, the basis of Marshall's cardinal utility analysis (utility measured in numbers called utils, or in money the consumer is willing to pay).
Reason: each particular want is satiable — as it gets satisfied, the urge for more weakens. Also, goods are imperfect substitutes for each other, so one good cannot satisfy every want.

Assumptions / limitations: (1) units consumed must be identical in size, quality and taste, and the consumer's habits and tastes must not change; (2) units must be of a standard, reasonable size — giving a very thirsty person water by the spoon may first show increasing MU; (3) consumption must be continuous, with no long time gap; (4) the law may not hold for money, gold or collections, where more may increase the desire (the miser, the stamp collector); (5) the MU of a good can be affected by the presence or absence of related goods (substitutes and complements).
concepts.analogy: The first glass of cold water on a hot day is heaven; the fifth is a chore.
concepts.work: Bundle pricing and "second unit at half price" offers exist because the consumer values the second unit less — firms price to the falling marginal utility.

concepts.title: Consumer surplus (Marshall)
body: Consumer surplus is the excess of what a consumer is willing to pay for a good over what he actually pays. Consumer surplus = total amount one is willing to pay − amount actually paid (= TU in money terms − price × quantity).

It rests on diminishing marginal utility. The consumer buys units until MU (in money) equals price. Every earlier unit is worth more than the price paid, so it yields a surplus; the marginal (last) unit yields none.

On a graph, consumer surplus is the area below the demand (MU) curve and above the price line, up to the quantity bought — a triangle for a straight-line demand curve. A rise in price shrinks consumer surplus; a fall in price enlarges it. Total market consumer surplus is the sum of individual surpluses.

Applications: helps firms in pricing (price discrimination tries to capture consumer surplus); helps government judge the welfare effect of taxes and subsidies and decide which projects (bridges, roads) to build; explains "value-for-money" comparisons between countries; and is used in cost–benefit analysis.

Limitations: utility cannot be measured precisely in cardinal numbers; the MU of money is assumed constant, which is unrealistic; it is hard to measure for necessities (willingness to pay may be almost infinite) and for prestige goods; and it ignores the effect of substitutes and complements on willingness to pay.
concepts.analogy: If you were ready to pay ₹500 for a concert ticket and got it for ₹300, the ₹200 "you saved in your mind" is your consumer surplus.
concepts.work: Dynamic pricing in airlines and cab aggregators is designed to capture part of consumer surplus — CAs reviewing revenue management policies see this concept in action.

concepts.title: Indifference curve approach: assumptions and the curve
body: The indifference curve (IC) approach, developed by Hicks and Allen, replaces the cardinal measurement of utility with an ordinal ranking: the consumer only needs to say whether he prefers one bundle to another or is indifferent between them.

Assumptions: the consumer is rational and seeks maximum satisfaction; utility is ordinal (ranked, not measured); preferences are consistent and transitive (if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C); more of a good is preferred to less (non-satiety); and there is a diminishing marginal rate of substitution.

An indifference schedule lists combinations of two goods that give the same satisfaction. Plotting it gives an indifference curve — the locus of all combinations among which the consumer is indifferent. A set of ICs is an indifference map; a higher (further right) curve shows a higher level of satisfaction.

MRSxy — the marginal rate at which X is substituted for Y — is the amount of Y the consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of X while staying on the same IC; it is the (absolute) slope of the IC: MRSxy = −ΔY/ΔX. As the consumer gets more X and less Y, he is willing to give up less and less Y for each extra X — diminishing MRS.
concepts.analogy: An indifference curve is a contour line on a map of happiness: every point on it is the same "height" of satisfaction.
concepts.work: Product-mix and bundle design (data vs talk-time in mobile plans, speed vs price in courier services) uses trade-off thinking identical to MRS.

concepts.title: Properties of indifference curves
body: (1) They slope downward from left to right — to keep satisfaction constant, more of X must mean less of Y. (2) They are convex to the origin — because MRSxy diminishes. (3) Two ICs never intersect — if they did, the point of intersection would give two different levels of satisfaction at once, which contradicts transitivity and "more is better". (4) A higher IC represents a higher level of satisfaction. (5) An IC does not touch either axis — the consumer is assumed to want some of both goods (an IC touching an axis would mean wanting only one good).
Special cases: perfect substitutes give straight-line ICs (constant MRS); perfect complements (left shoe and right shoe) give L-shaped ICs.
concepts.analogy: Contour lines of different heights on a map never cross — two heights at one point is impossible. ICs follow the same rule.
concepts.work: In valuation and pricing studies, consistency checks (no "crossing" preferences) are applied to survey data before relying on it — the same logic as non-intersecting ICs.

concepts.title: Budget line and consumer equilibrium
body: The budget line (price line) shows all combinations of two goods the consumer can buy by spending his whole income at given prices: Px·X + Py·Y = M. It meets the X-axis at M/Px and the Y-axis at M/Py, and its slope (absolute) is Px/Py. Points inside are affordable but leave money unspent; points outside are unaffordable.

Changes: a rise in income shifts the line outward parallel (a fall, inward); a change in the price of one good rotates (swivels) the line around the intercept of the other good — a fall in Px moves the X-intercept outward.

Consumer equilibrium: assumptions — a given indifference map, a fixed money income spent wholly on X and Y, given prices, homogeneous and divisible goods, and rational behaviour. The consumer reaches the highest IC his budget allows, which happens where the budget line is tangent to an IC. At that point the slope of the IC equals the slope of the budget line: MRSxy = Px/Py. The second condition is that the IC is convex to the origin at that point (MRS diminishing).
concepts.analogy: The budget line is a fence; the ICs are hills of happiness. You climb to the highest hill you can touch from inside the fence — where the fence just kisses a hill.
concepts.work: Personal financial planning by CAs is a budget-line exercise: the client's income fixes the frontier, and advice aims at the best mix of spending and saving within it.

illustrations.title: TU and MU schedule
illustrations.q: Rahul's total utility from glasses of juice is given. Compute marginal utility and identify (a) the point of satiety, (b) where disutility begins, (c) the stage where TU rises at a diminishing rate.

solution.text: (a) TU is maximum (37 utils) at the 5th and 6th glasses; MU of the 6th glass is 0 — the point of satiety. (b) The 7th glass has MU = -3: disutility. (c) From the 1st to the 5th glass TU rises while MU falls from 12 to 2 — rising at a diminishing rate.

illustrations.title: Consumer surplus from a schedule
illustrations.q: Meena is willing to pay ₹45, 38, 32, 27, 23, 20 and 16 for the 1st to 7th unit of a snack. The market price is ₹20. How many units does she buy, and what is her consumer surplus?

solution.text: She buys 6 units — up to the unit whose worth equals the price (₹20). The 7th unit (worth ₹16) is not bought. Consumer surplus = ₹185 − ₹120 = ₹65. The last unit bought gives zero surplus.

illustrations.title: Consumer surplus from a demand curve, and the effect of a price fall
illustrations.q: The market demand curve is P = 100 − 2Q. Find consumer surplus at a price of ₹40 and at ₹30, and the gain from the price fall.

solution.text: At P = 40: Q = (100 − 40) ÷ 2 = 30. Consumer surplus = ½ × base × height = ½ × 30 × (100 − 40) = ₹900.
Gain = ₹1,225 − ₹900 = ₹325. A lower price enlarges the triangle below the demand curve and above the price line.

checks.label: gain in consumer surplus from the price fall

illustrations.q: Combinations of apples (X) and bananas (Y) on one indifference curve are given. Compute MRSxy and comment.

illustrations.title: Budget line and consumer equilibrium
illustrations.q: A consumer has ₹1,200 to spend on X (₹40 each) and Y (₹30 each). (a) Write the budget equation and find the intercepts and slope. (b) At the bundle X = 15, Y = 20 her IC is tangent to the budget line. Verify it is affordable and state the equilibrium condition. (c) What happens if Px falls to ₹30?

solution.text: (b) Cost of (15, 20) = 40 × 15 + 30 × 20 = ₹1,200 — exactly the income, so it lies on the budget line. Since the IC is tangent there, MRSxy = Px/Py ≈ 1.33: she gives up about 1.33 Y for one more X, the same rate as the market. This is the equilibrium (highest attainable IC).
(c) The line swivels outward around the Y-intercept (40); the new X-intercept is 1,200 ÷ 30 = 40. She can reach a higher IC.

checks.label: max X when Px falls to ₹30

jobs.title: Designing a "buy 2, get the 3rd at half price" offer
jobs.role: CA in industry — commercial finance at an FMCG company
jobs.situation: Marketing proposes a multi-buy offer on a beverage. You are asked whether it makes economic sense.
steps: Recognise diminishing marginal utility: the 3rd bottle is worth less to the buyer than the 1st, so full price would not sell it.
A lower price on the extra unit matches the lower MU and induces extra purchases.
Check the margin: the half-price 3rd unit must still cover its variable cost.
Watch cannibalisation: some buyers would have bought three anyway, so you give away part of the margin.
jobs.takeaway: Multi-buy discounts are pricing to the falling marginal utility of extra units.

jobs.title: Toll pricing for a new bridge
jobs.role: CA in a public infrastructure consultancy
jobs.situation: A state government asks for a recommendation on the toll for a new bridge expected to carry 20,000 vehicles a day.
steps: Estimate the demand curve: how many vehicles at each toll.
Consumer surplus measures the benefit users get beyond the toll they pay — part of the social benefit of the bridge.
A very high toll collects revenue but destroys consumer surplus and diverts traffic; a lower toll raises welfare.
Present revenue, consumer surplus and total benefit at different tolls.
jobs.takeaway: Public projects are judged on consumer surplus, not only on revenue.

jobs.title: Explaining a household budget to a client
jobs.situation: A young client earning ₹80,000 a month wants to spend more on travel and also save for a house.
steps: Draw the budget line: travel vs savings within ₹80,000.
A rise in income shifts the line out; higher rent rotates it inward.
The best plan is where the client's trade-off (MRS) between travel and saving equals the "price" trade-off.
jobs.takeaway: Indifference-curve thinking helps clients see trade-offs clearly.

mcqs.q: In economics, utility means:
mcqs.explain: Utility is psychological and ethically neutral.

mcqs.q: Which is a characteristic of human wants?
options: Wants are unlimited, but a particular want is satiable
Each want can never be satisfied
mcqs.explain: Unlimited in number, but each one can be satisfied.

mcqs.q: Goods required because of social customs and habits, not for existence or efficiency, are:
mcqs.explain: They arise from habit or social convention.

mcqs.q: Nourishing food, clean water and education are examples of:
mcqs.explain: They raise productivity and energy.

mcqs.q: The classification of goods into necessaries, comforts and luxuries is:
options: Relative — it changes with person, place and time
mcqs.explain: Yesterday's luxury can be today's necessity.

mcqs.q: When total utility is maximum, marginal utility is:
mcqs.explain: Point of satiety.

mcqs.q: When marginal utility is negative, total utility:
mcqs.explain: Extra units reduce total satisfaction.

mcqs.q: TU from 1, 2 and 3 units is 12, 22 and 30 utils. MU of the 3rd unit is:
mcqs.explain: 30 − 22 = 8. 10 is the MU of the 2nd unit.

mcqs.q: At the first unit consumed:
mcqs.explain: TU of one unit is its MU.

mcqs.q: The law of diminishing marginal utility does NOT apply when:
options: There is a long time gap between consumption of units
mcqs.explain: Continuity is an assumption of the law.

mcqs.q: The law of diminishing marginal utility is generally said not to apply to:
options: Money and collections such as rare stamps
mcqs.explain: More money or a rarer collection may increase the desire.

mcqs.q: The cardinal utility approach is associated with:
mcqs.explain: Marshall measured utility in utils / money.

mcqs.q: Consumer surplus is the difference between:
options: What a consumer is willing to pay and what he actually pays
mcqs.explain: Marshall's definition.

mcqs.q: The concept of consumer surplus was propounded by:
mcqs.explain: Marshall.

mcqs.q: A consumer values successive units at ₹45, 38, 32, 27, 23, 20 and 16; price is ₹20. Consumer surplus is:
mcqs.explain: Buys 6 units; surplus = 25 + 18 + 12 + 7 + 3 + 0 = ₹65. ₹185 is total worth, ₹120 the amount paid; ₹61 wrongly buys the 7th unit (surplus −4).

mcqs.q: For the demand curve P = 100 − 2Q, consumer surplus at P = ₹40 is:
mcqs.explain: Q = 30; CS = ½ × 30 × 60 = ₹900. ₹1,800 forgets the ½; ₹1,200 is amount paid.

mcqs.q: A fall in the price of a good, other things constant, will:
mcqs.explain: The triangle under the demand curve above price grows.

mcqs.q: A limitation of consumer surplus is that it assumes:
mcqs.explain: MU of money is taken as constant, which is unrealistic.

mcqs.q: The indifference curve approach treats utility as:
options: Cardinal — it can be measured in numbers
mcqs.explain: Hicks and Allen: only rankings are needed.

mcqs.q: MRSxy refers to:
options: Units of Y given up for one more unit of X, keeping satisfaction constant
Units of X given up for one more Y at higher satisfaction
Ratio of TU of X and Y
Price of X divided by income
mcqs.explain: Slope of the IC.

mcqs.q: Combinations on an IC: (1 X, 20 Y), (2 X, 14 Y), (3 X, 10 Y). MRSxy between the 2nd and 3rd combination is:
mcqs.explain: 14 − 10 = 4 Y for one X. 6 is the MRS between the 1st and 2nd.

mcqs.q: Indifference curves are convex to the origin because of:
mcqs.explain: Diminishing MRS gives convexity.

mcqs.q: Two indifference curves cannot intersect because:
options: The intersection point would show two levels of satisfaction at once
mcqs.explain: This contradicts consistency and transitivity.

mcqs.q: Indifference curves for perfect complements are:
mcqs.explain: Goods used in fixed proportions.

mcqs.q: With income ₹1,200, Px = ₹40 and Py = ₹30, the maximum quantity of Y that can be bought is:
mcqs.explain: 1,200 ÷ 30 = 40. 30 is the maximum X.

mcqs.q: A rise in consumer's income, prices unchanged, causes the budget line to:
mcqs.explain: Both intercepts rise in the same proportion.

mcqs.q: A fall in the price of X only causes the budget line to:
mcqs.explain: Only the X-intercept moves out.

mcqs.q: At consumer equilibrium in the indifference curve approach:
mcqs.explain: Slope of IC = slope of budget line.

mcqs.q: The slope of the budget line equals:
options: The ratio of the prices of the two goods (Px/Py)
mcqs.explain: Absolute slope = Px/Py; it equals MRS only at equilibrium.

mcqs.q: In the consumer surplus schedule, the consumer stops buying where:
mcqs.explain: Beyond this, MU < price.

questions.q: TU from 1 to 6 units of a commodity is 20, 36, 48, 54, 54 and 50 utils. Compute MU, identify the point of satiety and explain the relationship between TU and MU.

model.text: Point of satiety: 5th unit (TU maximum at 54, MU = 0). TU rises at a diminishing rate while MU falls but is positive (units 1–4); TU is maximum when MU = 0; TU falls when MU is negative (6th unit, MU = −4).

remarks: Show MU for the first unit as equal to TU.
mistakes: Calling the 4th unit the point of satiety because TU first reaches 54 there — MU of the 4th unit is still 6.
tips: Mark the point where MU = 0 clearly.

questions.q: The demand curve for a museum visit is P = 150 − 5Q (P in ₹, Q visits per year). The ticket price is ₹50. Compute (a) visits, (b) amount spent, (c) total willingness to pay, and (d) consumer surplus. Show steps.

model.text: (c) Total willingness to pay = area under the demand curve up to Q = 20 = rectangle (50 × 20 = ₹1,000) + triangle (½ × 20 × 100 = ₹1,000) = ₹2,000.
(d) Consumer surplus = ₹2,000 − ₹1,000 = ₹1,000 (the triangle above the price line).

scheme.pt: Total willingness to pay (area under curve)

remarks: Drawing the triangle in rough work avoids sign errors.
mistakes: Forgetting the ½ in the triangle area.
tips: CS = ½ × Q × (maximum price − market price) for a straight-line demand curve.

checks.label: q2 Q at P = 50 for P = 150 − 5Q
q2 total willingness to pay (area under demand curve)

questions.q: Ravi has ₹2,400 to spend on X (₹60) and Y (₹40). (a) Find the intercepts and slope of his budget line. (b) Is the bundle (24 X, 30 Y) affordable? (c) At his chosen bundle on the budget line, his MRSxy is 2. Is he in equilibrium? If not, which way should he move?

model.text: (b) Cost = 60 × 24 + 40 × 30 = ₹2,640 > ₹2,400 — not affordable (it lies outside the budget line). (A bundle costing exactly ₹2,400, such as 24 X and 24 Y, would lie on the line.)

(c) Equilibrium needs MRSxy = Px/Py = 1.5. Here MRS = 2 > 1.5: he values one X at 2 Y, while the market charges only 1.5 Y. He gains by buying more X and less Y; as he does so, MRS diminishes until it equals 1.5.

scheme.pt: Correct direction of adjustment with reason

remarks: Direction of adjustment is where most students lose marks.
mistakes: Comparing MRS with Py/Px instead of Px/Py.
tips: If MRSxy > Px/Py, buy more X; if less, buy more Y.

summary: Wants: unlimited, satiable individually, competitive, complementary, relative; utility = want-satisfying power (not usefulness, no ethics).
Classification: necessaries (life, efficiency, conventional), comforts, luxuries — relative.
TU = ΣMU; MU = TUn − TUn−1; TU max ⇔ MU = 0; TU falls ⇔ MU < 0.
LDMU: assumptions — identical units, standard size, continuity, constant tastes; exceptions — money, collections, related goods.
Consumer surplus = willing to pay − actually paid; area under demand curve above price; Marshall.
IC: ordinal utility, MRS diminishing; properties — downward slope, convex, non-intersecting, higher = better, not touching axes.
Budget line Px·X + Py·Y = M; equilibrium where IC tangent to budget line: MRSxy = Px/Py.
remember: Income change → parallel shift; one price change → rotation.
Perfect substitutes: straight-line ICs; perfect complements: L-shaped.
traps: The point of satiety is where MU = 0, not where TU first reaches its highest number if MU is still positive.
Slope of budget line = Px/Py (not Py/Px).

quickref.v: ΣWTP − P × Q; linear demand: ½ × Q × (Pmax − P)
Px·X + Py·Y = M; intercepts M/Px, M/Py

viva.q: What is consumer surplus, and how is it measured?
viva.model: Consumer surplus is the excess of what a consumer is willing to pay for a good over what he actually pays. It is measured as total willingness to pay minus the amount actually paid; on a graph it is the triangle-shaped area lying under the demand curve but over the price line. The concept was given by Marshall.

viva.q: State any four properties of indifference curves.
viva.model: Indifference curves slope downward from left to right, they are convex to the origin because of diminishing marginal rate of substitution, two indifference curves never intersect, a curve lying higher means more satisfaction, and they do not touch either axis.

viva.q: What is the condition of consumer equilibrium in the indifference curve approach?
viva.model: The consumer is in equilibrium where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve. At that point the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y equals the price ratio Px by Py, and the indifference curve is convex to the origin.

viva.q: Does the law of diminishing marginal utility apply to money and collections like rare stamps?
viva.model: Generally no. The law may not apply to money, gold or collections such as rare stamps, because having more of them can increase the desire for still more, as with a miser or a collector.

cases.title: Isha's entertainment budget
cases.case: Isha loves watching films in theatres. In a month she is willing to pay ₹120 for the first show, ₹100 for the second, ₹85 for the third, ₹70 for the fourth, ₹60 for the fifth and ₹50 for the sixth. A multiplex charges ₹60 a ticket. Separately, she sets aside ₹3,000 a month for movies (₹300 a show at a premium hall) and snacks (₹150 a combo), and she chooses a bundle where her indifference curve touches this budget line.

mcqs.q: At ₹60 a ticket, how many shows does Isha watch?
mcqs.explain: She watches while willingness ≥ price: ₹120, 100, 85, 70, 60 — five shows. The sixth (₹50) is worth less than ₹60.

mcqs.q: Her consumer surplus at ₹60 a ticket is:
mcqs.explain: (60 + 40 + 25 + 10 + 0) = ₹135. ₹435 is total willingness to pay for five shows; ₹125 wrongly adds the 6th show (−10).

mcqs.q: If the ticket price falls to ₹50, her consumer surplus becomes:
mcqs.explain: Six shows: 70 + 50 + 35 + 20 + 10 + 0 = ₹185 — a fall in price increases consumer surplus.

mcqs.q: On her premium-hall budget line, the maximum number of shows (no snacks) is:
mcqs.explain: 3,000 ÷ 300 = 10. 20 is the maximum snacks.

mcqs.q: At her chosen bundle, her MRS of shows for snacks equals:
mcqs.explain: MRS = P(shows)/P(snacks) = 300/150 = 2 snacks per show.
